Issued at 256 PM EDT Tue Aug 18 2026

Currently...Outflow produced by storms along the northern Gulf 
coast yesterday has traveled to Central Florida and helped get an 
early start to showers and lightning storms in the surge of 
moisture gradually sagging south across the peninsula. This line 
has already pushed through the Orlando Metro and is working 
through the southern counties. So far the primary storm hazard has
been frequent cloud to ground lightning and gusts to around 40 
mph, but the environment to the south could support stronger 
storms.

Rest of Today-Tonight...Offshore (WNW-WSW) flow continues as a 
nearly stationary front draped from the Deep South to the Mid 
Atlantic seaboard and a broad trough sliding over the eastern US 
keep the Bermuda high suppressed. GOES imagery shows a 
considerable moisture gradient across the Florida peninsula with 
PWATs less than 1.5" (0.5-0.75" below normal) over South Florida 
increasing to 2.15" (0.1-0.25" above normal) over North Florida, 
and the edge of the 2" PWATs sagging south through Central 
Florida. Models have struggled to capture the showers and storms 
riding the outflow in the higher moisture, making near storm 
environment analysis a challenge, and offering little help with 
convective evolution the rest of the afternoon. Earlier storms 
weren't able to live up to their full potential since the early 
start meant less instability from daytime heating. However, as the
storms and outflow push south they will move into higher 
instability. But then, the drier air to the south will be an 
increasingly significant hurdle to deep convection. To further 
complicate matters, the offshore flow and outflow has delayed or 
even impeded the onshore push of the east coast sea breeze. The 
boundary is likely to remain offshore from the Cape north, and may
only be able to make a brief inland push to the south before 
storms and outflow arrive. Where the sea breeze can move inland 
will be the greatest potential for strong storms with gusts to 55 
mph, in addition to frequent cloud to ground lightning and 
torrential downpours. Radar shows the boundary has begun a push 
near Sebastian inlet. Can't rule out stronger storms elsewhere, 
but chances are lower. Storms and heavy rainfall that get hung up 
on the boundary could produce locally heavy rainfall, though 
steering flow appears sufficient to keep the risk minimal. 

The early rain start has at least provided respite from the heat 
for the northern counties where cloud cover remains, with many 
sites in and around the Orlando Metro reporting temperatures in 
the 80s rather than 90s. Temperatures could get back into the 90s 
if skies clear, but will likely fall short of the M-U90s 
previously forecast. That said, the rain may spike dew points and 
result in some hot, sultry conditions. Areas that don't get rain, 
or where skies clear quickly, are forecast to reach the M-U90s 
with peak afternoon heat indices to around 112F, and a Heat 
Advisory remains in effect for all of East Central Florida until 8
PM.

Wednesday-Monday (Modified Previous Discussion)...An active 
pattern will continue across east central Florida through this 
week and into early next week. Mid-level ridging will weaken 
across the Florida peninsula, with guidance still developing a 
mid-level low over the eastern Gulf/Florida, before getting 
absorbed by a trough digging southward across the eastern US this 
weekend. At the surface, this mid-level pattern would support 
persistent increasing moisture locally, with a series of decaying 
frontal boundaries anticipated to approach Florida through late 
this week while broad high pressure remains situated across the 
Gulf. Locally, west to southwest winds are forecast to continue 
areawide, with daytime heating supporting the development of the 
east coast sea breeze each day. The push inland during the 
afternoon hours will result in winds becoming more south to 
southeasterly behind it, with westerly winds aloft preventing too 
much intrusion inland. Combined with the moist air mass in place, 
a diurnal pattern of showers and storms will persist, with 
development driven primarily by the sea breezes each day. Rain and
storm chances will remain near to above normal (40-60%) through 
the period, with storm hazards including lightning strikes, gusty 
winds, and heavy downpours that have the potential to produce 
minor, localized flooding in some spots. With steering flow 
remaining out of the west, activity will push offshore through the
afternoon and evening hours each day, with mostly dry conditions 
anticipated across the peninsula through the overnight hours.

Temperatures are forecast to remain above normal over the next
couple of days, then the increasing cloud cover and rain chances
will lead to a trend closer to normal late this week and into the
weekend. However, heat will still remain a concern through this
